rv.q: Here again, with the original cast intact, is laughter, erupting continuously throughout Mark Gatiss’s impeccable production.
Social awkwardness is a staple of British comedy and there is much about The Unfriend that is very amusing, although some set pieces feel rather over-engineered.
None of the teasing or nudging lands much of a point, and edginess quickly evaporates.
‘The Unfriend’ is unexciting, unadventurous and too often unfunny.
The Unfriend keeps you mirthfully on edge up to the final curtain.
The dialogue is admirably witty and inventive, and there are passages that would not disgrace Noël Coward.
The Unfriend is more multifaceted than it may first seem, as much as it is a comedy of manners it is also a comedy of menace.

Overall, there’s nothing wrong with the extended sitcom episode vibe that this production brings, but given this a 1 hour 40 minutes play with steep West End prices at the premium end, the question is whether it’s really worth it and if you’ll remember it the next day.

cn.t: Moffat and Gatiss' stage debut comedy-thriller earns mostly positive reviews for its humor and Frances Barber's scene-stealing performance, though some critics find the script half-baked and the sitcom-style execution uneven.
